Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't deal with even the slightest upset
Nothing good can happen to me anymore
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The trigger items are not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of police violence. Snake-related cues and fire/flames do not plausibly connect to police violence unless there were unusual event details, and no other selected items suggest such a context. This makes the trigger profile hard to explain for the same trauma.

Within Memory, 'Vivid Memory' and 'Memory Gaps' can coexist in PTSD, but 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with a severe PTSD presentation and with the memory disturbance pattern implied by the other memory items. It suggests unusually easy narrative access despite simultaneously endorsing vivid re-experiencing and amnestic gaps, which is internally inconsistent here.

Fire/flames is hard to reconcile as a trauma trigger for police violence in the absence of any corroborating memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to fire; 'Police' as an authority trigger fits, but 'fire/flames' appears trauma-incongruent for this profile.

issues.item: Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
issues.explanation: The Memory node contains a direct internal contradiction: endorsing very clear/detailed memories, irretrievable gaps, and very easy verbal access all together is not clinically coherent as stated. Vivid memory can coexist with some gaps, but pairing both with 'I can talk about what happened very easily' strongly conflicts with a severe PTSD profile and with the fragmented/distressing memory pattern implied by the other memory items.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked trauma-memory disruption indicated by both severe memory gaps and fragmented, disconnected recollections. Those memory items imply impaired coherent access to the trauma narrative, making very easy verbal access hard to reconcile clinically in the same profile.

vignette:
When Asha Patel was stopped by police at seventy-two, she had been leaving a client's townhouse with a portfolio of fabric swatches tucked under her arm, still thinking about paint samples and lamp placement. A neighbor had reported "a suspicious person" entering the property. The officers approached before she had fully understood they were speaking to her. What stayed with her was not a single clear sequence but flashes: the hard command in a male voice, the sight of dark uniforms closing around her, her cheek against rough concrete, the abrasive scrape of the pavement and the weave of an officer's glove against her wrist as her hands were forced behind her back. She recalls trying to explain that she was the interior designer, that the homeowner knew her, but when she speaks of it now she stops and presses her lips together. She says she knows what happened and yet cannot find words for the worst parts. The memory comes in jagged pieces, with blank stretches in between that she cannot fill no matter how long she sits with it.

In the weeks afterward, the event did not settle into the past. The roughness of certain upholstery fabrics in her studio, the stiff texture of coarse canvas, even a heavily napped rug could bring her up short with a surge in her chest before she had time to think. Seeing police officers outside municipal buildings or a uniformed security presence near a design showroom made her body tense and her breathing turn shallow. She had come to believe that these reactions proved something had broken in her permanently. If a glimpse of a uniform or the brush of a particular texture could undo her so quickly, then in her mind she could no longer handle even small upsets. She began saying to herself that her body had become her enemy, reacting as if she were still pinned down even in ordinary places, and from there it was a short step to the conviction that nothing good was ahead for her now.

Those conclusions changed how she moved through her days. Asha started scanning for police cars when she drove to client meetings, crossing streets to avoid officers on sidewalks and lingering in her car if she saw dark uniforms near a building entrance. At work she became wary of her own materials, asking an assistant to unpack rough textiles or set aside certain fabric books without explaining why. The more certain she became that she could not cope and that her body would betray her, the more threatening those cues felt. A routine visit to a downtown apartment building could seem dangerous simply because a security guard wore clothing close enough to a police uniform to set her on edge. By then it was not only the original triggers that frightened her, but what they seemed to say about her: that she was fragile now, always one encounter away from losing control.

Her beliefs about herself also shaped what happened when she tried to remember. When family members encouraged her to "tell it from the beginning," Asha would falter quickly, overwhelmed by the sense that she could not bear what came up. She would abandon the effort, saying there was no point because her mind no longer worked the way it should. The story stayed broken into disconnected images partly because each attempt confirmed, for her, that she was too easily upset to hold the memory steady. She interpreted the blank places and her inability to put the experience into words as further evidence that she was damaged beyond repair and that even her own mind could not be relied upon.

Over time, those fractured recollections made the world feel even less predictable. Because the event remained a set of sensory shards rather than a complete story, a texture or uniform could hit her with the force of something happening again, not something remembered. The missing stretches left her unable to reassure herself about what had happened and ended, and the disconnected fragments made police presence especially potent: a glimpse of navy fabric, a badge, the feel of coarse material under her fingers was enough to call up a bodily certainty of danger before thought caught up. She became increasingly reluctant to take projects in government buildings, courthouses, or upscale condos with visible security, narrowing her work in a way clients noticed. A few longtime clients drifted elsewhere after she cancelled site visits at the last minute.

Now, widowed and living alone, Asha has come for help after turning down a major commission because the property was across from a police precinct. She was ashamed of how quickly she said no and frightened by what that refusal seemed to confirm. What scares her most is the sense that her life has been reduced by these reactions-that her body will keep sounding an alarm she cannot control, that the memory will remain unspeakable and in pieces, and that the future has closed down around that moment on the pavement. What she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is to be able to walk into her own work again without bracing for danger at every uniform, every rough surface, every reminder that her mind and body still behave as if she is not safe.
